paragraphs: Connecting two existing molecules requires designing a small molecular linker that fits both partners. This differs from generating an entire molecule freely: the proposed connector must respect the given structures, choose suitable attachment atoms, and account for how the molecules sit in three-dimensional space. Attachment locations are themselves unknown beforehand.

3DLinker addresses these decisions together through a conditional graph variational autoencoder. It predicts the anchor atoms and generates both the linker's graph structure and its three-dimensional coordinates. Its E(3) equivariance makes the geometric modeling consistent with changes in spatial orientation and position. This matters because a plausible connectivity pattern alone does not resolve the geometric constraints involved in connecting the molecules without atom clashes.

The authors compare 3DLinker with conditional generative models adapted from other molecular design tasks. They report a significantly higher molecular-graph recovery rate and accurate prediction of all atoms' coordinates. These findings support treating attachment selection, chemical connectivity, and spatial structure as coupled parts of the linker-generation problem.
icml-2022-3dlinker-an-e-3-equivariant-va.tldr: 3DLinker jointly predicts molecular attachment atoms, linker connectivity, and three-dimensional structure using an equivariant generative model.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that carry out natural-language goals by operating a computer through a keyboard and mouse. The interface matters because it connects machine actions to the same kinds of interactions people perform. Human-computer interaction data can therefore inform how an agent behaves while it learns to complete tasks.

The proposed approach combines reinforcement learning with behavioral priors drawn from actual human interactions. Those priors supply information about human behavior, while reinforcement learning develops task-solving ability. The work centers on making this combination scalable, rather than building the approach around individually designed learning curricula or specialized action spaces for particular tasks.

On MiniWob++, the authors report state-of-the-art results and human-level mean performance across the benchmark's tasks, alongside strong evidence of transfer between tasks. The mean-performance result describes aggregate achievement across this suite. The findings support the usefulness of a shared human-agent interface and suggest a route toward broader computer control; competency beyond MiniWob++ is presented as a prospect.
icml-2022-a-data-driven-approach-for-lea.tldr: Combining reinforcement learning with human interaction priors achieves human-level mean performance on the MiniWob++ computer-control benchmark.

paragraphs: A familiar temporal pattern can remain recognizable when played faster or slower. This paper builds that kind of generalization into SITHCon, a deep convolutional network for time-series tasks. The central question is whether a model can recognize a learned pattern at unfamiliar speeds without learning new weights for each speed.

SITHCon represents time using logarithmic compression at every level. In this representation, stretching or compressing an input's timing becomes a shift along the log-time axis. The network uses the translation invariance of its convolutional output to handle that shift. This connects a change in temporal scale to a transformation the architecture is designed to accommodate.

The authors evaluate classification and regression with both single-variable and multivariable time series. Compared with a Temporal Convolution Network, SITHCon generalizes robustly across time rescalings spanning roughly an order of magnitude. They also show generalization across exponentially large scales by extending the temporal memory's range without retraining weights. Thus, the broader range comes with an explicit change to memory coverage.
icml-2022-a-deep-convolutional-neural-ne.tldr: SITHCon uses logarithmic temporal memory to recognize learned time-series patterns across substantial changes in playback speed.

paragraphs: A neural network's weight matrix determines how it processes information. In many conventional networks, training adjusts that matrix and runtime use leaves it fixed. This paper revisits a different arrangement: a self-referential weight matrix that can rapidly modify all of itself while the network is running.

The proposed SRWM builds on fast weight programmers and closely related linear Transformers. It learns to perform its own modifications through outer products and the delta update rule. The contribution is a scalable mechanism for learned runtime changes to the matrix itself. Such architectures could, in principle, support recursive forms of learning how to learn, but that possibility is distinct from the experiments reported here.

The authors test SRWM on supervised few-shot learning and multitask reinforcement learning in procedurally generated game environments. They report practical applicability and competitive performance in these settings. These results establish that the proposed self-modification mechanism can serve as a useful working architecture, giving practical evidence for an idea that had previously received little experimental study.
icml-2022-a-modern-self-referential-weig.tldr: SRWM learns to modify its own weight matrix during runtime and shows competitive results in few-shot learning and multitask reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: An agent's observations can contain far more information than its decisions require, especially when signals are noisy and the environment is only partially observable. This paper seeks a minimal state representation that retains enough information for choosing actions. It calls these compact decision-relevant descriptions Action-Sufficient state Representations, or ASRs.

The method starts with a generative environment model describing structural relationships among system variables. It characterizes the desired representations through those structural constraints and the policy-learning objective of maximizing cumulative reward. A structured sequential variational autoencoder then estimates the environment model and extracts ASRs. This ties representation learning to the information needed for control, rather than treating every observed detail as equally relevant.

Experiments in CarRacing and VizDoom show a clear advantage from learning and using ASRs for policy learning. The estimated model also lets the agent learn from imagined outcomes within the compact latent space, improving sample efficiency. Together, these findings connect compact representation learning with both better policy learning and more efficient use of experience.
icml-2022-action-sufficient-state-repres.tldr: The paper learns compact, structurally constrained state representations that retain decision-relevant information and support learning from imagined outcomes.

paragraphs: This paper studies bandit learning when losses can have unusually large extremes, including cases where variance does not exist. Its assumption is that a moment of order alpha, with alpha greater than one and at most two, is bounded by a scale parameter. The analysis covers both stochastic and adversarial environments.

The first algorithm, HTINF, achieves optimal regret in both environments when the tail parameters are known, without needing to know which environment it faces. Regret measures the accumulated disadvantage relative to the comparison choice. When the parameters are unknown, HTINF instead has logarithmic-style, instance-dependent regret in stochastic cases and sublinear regret in adversarial cases. Sublinear regret means the average disadvantage vanishes as the horizon grows.

A second algorithm, AdaTINF, achieves minimax-optimal regret without knowing either tail parameter, even in the adversarial setting. Its guarantee matches a known lower bound established under the more informative stochastic setup. The contribution therefore separates adaptation to environment type from adaptation to unknown loss-tail characteristics, providing guarantees for both challenges.
icml-2022-adaptive-best-of-both-worlds-a.tldr: HTINF and AdaTINF provide regret guarantees for heavy-tailed bandits while adapting to environment type or unknown tail parameters.

paragraphs: Optimizing a black-box system can involve two kinds of variables: design choices that can be controlled and environmental conditions that fluctuate outside the decision-maker's control. A useful design must account for those fluctuations. Chance-constrained optimization expresses this by maximizing expected performance while requiring constraints to hold with a specified probability.

The paper addresses an additional uncertainty: the environmental probability distribution may itself be imprecisely known. It proposes a Bayesian optimization method for the distributionally robust version of the chance-constrained problem. This formulation incorporates uncertainty about the distribution into the search for a design, so the optimization is not based solely on one precisely specified environmental model.

The authors show that the proposed method can obtain a solution with arbitrarily high accuracy, with high probability, after finitely many trials. This is a probabilistic accuracy guarantee for the studied problem, rather than a claim that every run must succeed. Numerical experiments further support the method's usefulness for black-box optimization with uncertain environments and probabilistic constraints.
icml-2022-bayesian-optimization-for-dist.tldr: The paper develops Bayesian optimization for probabilistic constraints when the distribution of uncontrollable environmental variables is uncertain.

paragraphs: Datamodeling asks how the choice of training examples shapes a model's prediction on one fixed target example. For a fixed dataset and learning algorithm, a datamodel takes the membership of a training subset as input. It predicts the outcome of training on that subset and evaluating the resulting model on the target.

This replaces a complicated training-and-evaluation process with a function of which examples were included. The authors show that even linear datamodels can successfully predict model outputs despite the complexity of the underlying neural-network training. The finding concerns the usefulness of this approximation; it does not require the trained neural network itself to be linear.

The paper demonstrates several uses of this perspective: predicting the consequences of changing a dataset, detecting brittle predictions, finding semantically related examples, and quantifying train-test leakage. Datamodels also produce rich representations of data. These applications share a common idea: examples can be understood through the effects their inclusion has on predictions, linking model behavior directly to training-set composition.
icml-2022-datamodels-understanding-predi.tldr: Datamodels predict how training-set membership affects model outputs, enabling analysis of dataset changes, brittle predictions, and relationships between examples.

paragraphs: Generating all translation tokens in parallel can reduce decoding latency, but independent token predictions struggle with dependencies among words. This becomes especially important when a sentence admits multiple translations: the model needs to represent alternatives while preserving the relationships that make each alternative coherent. DA-Transformer changes the structure used to represent those possibilities.

The model organizes hidden states into a directed acyclic graph. Each path through that graph corresponds to a particular translation, while the graph as a whole represents multiple translations simultaneously. This gives the model a structured way to capture alternatives and their token dependencies while retaining fast, non-autoregressive prediction.

On raw WMT training data, DA-Transformer improves over previous non-autoregressive Transformers by about three BLEU points on average. The authors also report competitive results with autoregressive Transformers without knowledge distillation, describing this as a first for a non-autoregressive model. The findings show that graph-structured alternatives can substantially improve translation quality within the parallel-generation approach in the evaluated setting.
icml-2022-directed-acyclic-transformer-f.tldr: DA-Transformer represents alternative translations as graph paths, improving parallel translation quality without relying on knowledge distillation.

paragraphs: Self-attention relates input tokens to one another, but the tokens impose a fixed scale for those relationships. A single token may be too narrow a unit for some higher-level dependencies. ContextPool addresses this by letting each token gather an adaptively sized neighborhood of information before the attention computation.

The module learns both how strongly neighboring features should contribute and how large the pooling region should be. Different tokens can therefore enter attention with context gathered at different scales. Inspired by pooling in convolutional networks, this approach changes the content and granularity of the representations that attention operates on.

The authors find that ContextPool increases expressiveness and often enables strong performance with fewer layers, reducing computation. Across several language and image benchmarks, Transformers equipped with the module match or exceed state-of-the-art performance while using less compute. They also outperform evaluated approaches that learn context sizes or sparse attention patterns. The module applies to convolutional networks as well, supporting its use as a broader method for efficient feature learning.
icml-2022-efficient-representation-learn.tldr: ContextPool learns a different pooling scale for each token before attention, improving representation quality with reduced computation in evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Choosing a pretrained model, and deciding which layers to transfer, requires estimating how useful its features will be for a new task. Training every candidate extensively can make that selection expensive. TransRate provides a transferability score from a single pass over labeled examples of the target task.

The score estimates the mutual information between extracted features and target labels, using coding rate as an efficient substitute for entropy. Its interpretation combines completeness and compactness: whether the features retain enough task-relevant information, and whether examples from each class form sufficiently compact feature groups. These two properties connect the score to both information preservation and generalization.

The authors provide theoretical analysis linking TransRate to performance after transfer learning. They also evaluate it across 35 pretrained models and 16 downstream tasks, reporting strong performance despite an implementation of only ten lines. The practical contribution is an inexpensive basis for comparing models and layers before committing to transfer training, supported by both analysis and broad empirical evaluation.
icml-2022-frustratingly-easy-transferabi.tldr: TransRate estimates the transferability of pretrained features in one pass using an efficient information-based score.

paragraphs: A graph's meaning should not depend on how its nodes are numbered or its adjacency matrix is ordered. Graph neural networks commonly enforce this through permutation-invariant message aggregation. However, such aggregation can overlook relationships between neighboring nodes, reducing the structural information available to the network.

This paper introduces an efficient permutation-sensitive aggregation mechanism built using permutation groups. The mechanism captures pairwise correlations among neighbors while addressing the overarching requirement of graph-isomorphism invariance. The key distinction is between preserving the identity of the graph under relabeling and retaining useful relationships within a node's neighborhood.

The authors prove that their approach has strictly greater distinguishing power than the two-dimensional Weisfeiler-Lehman test and at least the power of the three-dimensional test. They also establish linear sampling complexity. Experiments on multiple synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate the model's superiority in the reported evaluations. The theoretical and empirical results together support capturing neighbor relationships as a way to improve graph representations without requiring an inefficient sampling mechanism.
icml-2022-going-deeper-into-permutation-.tldr: Permutation-group aggregation captures relationships among graph neighbors with proven expressive power at least matching the 3-WL test.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes provide uncertainty estimates, but their cubic cost in the number of observations limits scalability. Sparse approximations use a smaller collection of inducing points to represent the model. Those points control flexibility, and some tasks still require many of them, leaving a substantial computational burden.

This paper makes the inducing points depend on the current input. A neural network receives a data instance and produces both inducing-point locations and the parameters of the approximate posterior distribution. Computation is thereby shared through the neural network, while the resulting sparse representation adapts to individual inputs. This addresses the need for a large fixed collection of inducing points.

Across several experiments, the method performs similarly to or better than other state-of-the-art sparse variational Gaussian processes while drastically reducing the number of inducing points. The authors report faster training and prediction and the ability to scale to larger datasets. These findings connect input-specific flexibility with lower computational cost, rather than requiring model flexibility to come solely from increasing the inducing-point count.
icml-2022-input-dependent-sparse-gaussia.tldr: A neural network generates input-specific inducing points and posterior parameters, reducing sparse Gaussian-process costs while maintaining strong empirical performance.

paragraphs: Inferring a decision-maker's priorities from observed actions becomes harder when their knowledge changes over time. A fixed behavioral model can miss that evolution. This paper focuses on learning interpretable accounts of changing decisions from offline data, motivated by questions about how clinical practice and organ-allocation policies develop.

The authors model evolving decision-making with contextual bandits and formulate the inverse problem: using observed behavior to learn a representation of the agent's changing behavior and knowledge. They propose two algorithms, one learning a parametric representation and the other a nonparametric representation. Both address the need to describe nonstationary behavior rather than assume a single unchanging policy.

The methods are evaluated using real and simulated liver-transplantation data. These studies illustrate applicability and explainability, and they benchmark and validate algorithmic accuracy. The contribution is a framework for examining how decision processes evolve from historical observations. In the motivating setting, that provides a way to study changes in allocation behavior alongside changes in the decision-maker's understanding of the world.
icml-2022-inverse-contextual-bandits-lea.tldr: Inverse Contextual Bandits learns interpretable representations of how decision-makers' behavior and knowledge evolve from offline observations.

paragraphs: Graph-based combinatorial optimization often relies on heuristics because exact solutions are difficult to obtain. Even heuristics can become expensive on large graphs. LeNSE tackles this cost by searching for a smaller subgraph where an existing heuristic can run quickly while retaining a high likelihood of finding a near-optimal solution for the original problem.

Its central component is a reinforcement-learning algorithm that navigates possible subgraphs using a Euclidean embedding as a map. The embedding is trained with an existing heuristic applied to only a small part of the original graph. This combines learned selection of where to search with the problem-solving ability of established heuristics.

The authors test vertex cover, max-cut, and influence maximization on real graphs containing up to ten million edges. The selected subgraphs yield solutions comparable to applying the heuristics to the entire graph, at a fraction of the runtime. These are empirical results showing that a carefully selected smaller search region can preserve solution quality while substantially reducing the work required.
icml-2022-lense-learning-to-navigate-sub.tldr: LeNSE learns to select small subgraphs where existing optimization heuristics achieve comparable solutions much faster in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Adding more kinds of input does not always improve a jointly trained neural network. The paper investigates why a multimodal network can perform worse than the strongest network using just one modality, even though multiple signals offer more information. Its proposed explanation is competition between modalities during learning.

The proof uses a simplified data distribution and a late-fusion network with smoothed ReLU activations trained by gradient descent. Under this setup, only a subset of modalities is learned by the corresponding encoders. The remaining modalities lose the competition, leaving useful features undiscovered and creating suboptimal joint-training behavior. In comparable unimodal learning settings, the authors prove that networks learn features associated with their own modality.

Experiments illustrate that this competition also matches behavior observed in late-fusion joint training, supplementing the theoretical account. The contribution is a concrete mechanism linking training dynamics to underused input information. Its proof is tied to the stated distribution, architecture, and learning procedure; it explains a studied failure mode rather than establishing that multimodal training must always fail.
icml-2022-modality-competition-what-make.tldr: Under a specified theoretical setup, jointly trained modalities compete so that some encoders fail to learn useful features.

paragraphs: Predicting expert human play and playing strongly are related but distinct goals. Imitation learning can reproduce human choices yet still make costly mistakes. Search and self-play can produce strong decisions whose style differs substantially from human behavior. This paper combines imitation with search to address both objectives together.

The search procedure penalizes KL divergence from a policy learned through imitation. This penalty encourages the searched policy to remain close to human behavioral patterns while search improves decisions. In chess and Go, the authors find that this regularized search both predicts strong humans more accurately and plays better than imitation learning alone.

The paper also introduces a regret-minimization algorithm with regularization based on the same divergence from an imitation policy. Used for search in no-press Diplomacy, it matches imitation learning's human-action prediction accuracy while producing a substantially stronger policy. The results show different benefits across the evaluated games: improved prediction and strength in chess and Go, and preserved prediction accuracy with greater strength in Diplomacy.
icml-2022-modeling-strong-and-human-like.tldr: Search regularized toward an imitation-learned policy improves playing strength while preserving or improving human-action prediction in the evaluated games.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive Transformers seek faster text generation by predicting an entire sentence in parallel. That speed comes with a learning challenge: the model loses the usual left-to-right mechanism for relating token choices. This paper analyzes what information can disappear during training and why existing alternative objectives can help.

The authors show that straightforward likelihood maximization can approximate individual token distributions while discarding dependencies between tokens. They quantify the discarded information using the dataset's conditional total correlation. This gives a precise way to describe why modeling plausible tokens individually can still fail to represent how those tokens belong together.

The paper then places many previous training objectives in a common framework. Their success is explained through likelihood maximization on a proxy distribution that reduces information loss. Empirical studies support this interpretation of observed learning behavior and show that it can guide new training methods. The contribution is both a diagnosis of the dependence problem and a shared explanation for methods that mitigate it.
icml-2022-on-the-learning-of-non-autoreg.tldr: The paper explains non-autoregressive training difficulties through lost token dependencies and unifies successful objectives as learning from proxy distributions.

paragraphs: Learning-augmented algorithms use machine-learned predictions to improve traditional decision procedures. The goal is to benefit when predictions are accurate while retaining worst-case guarantees when they are unreliable. Caching is a natural setting for this idea because decisions must be made despite uncertainty about future requests.

This paper adds a resource question: how often does the algorithm actually need to use predictions? It introduces a setting in which prediction use is deliberately limited and studies that setting for caching. The focus is therefore on obtaining the value of predictive information while reducing the amount of such information consumed.

The authors show that quantitatively similar results are possible with only a sublinear number of predictions. Sublinear use means the prediction count grows more slowly than the scale of the request sequence. The result establishes that prediction access need not grow proportionally to every caching decision to retain comparable learning-augmented guarantees. It makes prediction usage itself part of the algorithm-design problem, alongside performance when predictions are accurate or inaccurate.
icml-2022-parsimonious-learning-augmente.tldr: Learning-augmented caching can retain quantitatively similar guarantees while using only a sublinear number of predictions.

paragraphs: Plug-and-play image restoration inserts a denoiser into an iterative optimization algorithm in place of a proximal operator. Deep denoisers can produce strong visual results, but proving that the resulting iterations converge has been difficult. Existing analyses often rely on restrictive denoiser properties or strongly convex data-fitting terms.

The paper builds on denoisers trained to act as a gradient-descent step on a neural-network-parameterized function. It shows that such a gradient denoiser can also correspond to the proximal operator of another scalar function. This connection allows the authors to apply nonconvex proximal-optimization theory to plug-and-play proximal gradient descent and alternating direction methods.

For constructions based on a smooth gradient denoiser, the authors establish convergence of PnP-PGD and PnP-ADMM toward stationary points of an explicit objective. A stationary-point guarantee is weaker than a guarantee of reaching a global optimum. Numerical experiments in deblurring, super-resolution, and inpainting confirm the convergence results, linking a useful denoising construction to a clearer account of what its iterations optimize.
icml-2022-proximal-denoiser-for-converge.tldr: Interpreting a smooth gradient denoiser as a proximal operator yields convergence guarantees for two plug-and-play methods toward stationary points.

paragraphs: Density estimation aims to describe how observations are distributed, but anomalous data can distort that description. This paper introduces MoM-KDE, a nonparametric estimator combining kernel density estimation with the median-of-means principle. Its purpose is to retain useful density estimates in the presence of a broad class of anomalies, including potentially adversarial data.

The theoretical contribution is a set of finite-sample error bounds that hold with high probability without requiring prior knowledge of the outliers. These guarantees concern errors at a finite amount of data, going beyond consistency results available only under very specific contamination models. The robustness claim remains tied to the class of anomalous data covered by the analysis.

The authors also develop an influence function adapted to their OUI framework to examine robustness. In comparisons with other robust kernel estimators, MoM-KDE achieves competitive results with significantly lower computational complexity. Taken together, the analysis and comparisons present a method that combines explicit error guarantees under contamination with a computational advantage over the evaluated alternatives.
icml-2022-robust-kernel-density-estimati.tldr: MoM-KDE combines kernel density estimation with median-of-means robustness, providing finite-sample guarantees and competitive results at lower computational complexity.

paragraphs: Quantization reduces the numerical precision used by a neural network to make deployment more efficient. Mixed-precision quantization assigns different bitwidths to different layers or modules. Finding those assignments can be costly, while selecting them from partial prior knowledge can introduce bias or yield suboptimal choices.

SDQ learns the precision strategy through stochastic differentiable quantization. Its differentiable bitwidth parameters determine probabilities for quantizing between adjacent bitwidths, providing a smoother gradient approximation for learning the assignments. After acquiring the strategy, the network receives further training with entropy-aware bin regularization and knowledge distillation. The approach thus combines learning where to allocate precision with subsequent refinement of the quantized network.

The authors evaluate SDQ across networks, datasets, GPUs, and FPGA hardware. They report outperforming the compared state-of-the-art mixed- and single-precision methods while using lower bitwidths. Across various ResNet and MobileNet families, results even exceed the original full-precision counterparts. These empirical findings support the effectiveness of jointly learning precision choices and refining the resulting low-precision model.
icml-2022-sdq-stochastic-differentiable-.tldr: SDQ learns mixed-precision bitwidths through stochastic differentiable quantization and reports strong accuracy at reduced precision.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization methods differ in how they sample data, compute gradients, and exchange information between devices. This paper puts several such methods into one framework for empirical risk minimization. Its central representation is an augmented graph whose nodes model samples and whose edges encode both local gradient computation and communication across devices.

Choosing different graph topologies recovers methods including Local-SGD and decentralized SGD. The same perspective also covers variance-reduction and gradient-tracking methods such as SAGA, Local-SVRG, and GT-SAGA. A structured Lyapunov function supports a shared convergence analysis for smooth convex and strongly convex objectives, recovering the best known rates for many existing algorithms.

The analysis distinguishes two sources of data heterogeneity. Variance reduction can eliminate its effects within devices, while gradient tracking can eliminate its effects across devices, enabling exact convergence to the optimal solution under the analyzed conditions. Numerical experiments confirm the findings. The framework therefore explains both relationships among algorithms and the different roles their corrective mechanisms play when data are unevenly distributed.
icml-2022-tackling-data-heterogeneity-a-.tldr: An augmented sample graph unifies stochastic optimization methods and explains how variance reduction and gradient tracking address different forms of data heterogeneity.

paragraphs: A linear layer trained by gradient descent can be expressed as a memory of its training experience and initial weights. In this dual form, outputs arise through unnormalized dot-product attention over stored training information. The paper revisits this known mathematical view as a tool for understanding neural-network predictions.

The attraction is interpretability: examining the attention weights offers a way to visualize how a network uses training patterns at test time. The practical difficulty is that the representation's size, time cost, and space cost grow linearly with the number of training patterns. That growth has hindered direct study of networks in this form.

The authors investigate small-scale supervised image classification in single-task, multitask, and continual-learning settings, as well as language modeling. They discuss both the potential and limits of using the dual view to interpret reliance on training patterns. The contribution is an experimental exploration of a mathematically grounded connection between predictions and training experience, with the scaling burden remaining an explicit part of that perspective.
icml-2022-the-dual-form-of-neural-networ.tldr: The paper explores a dual representation of trained linear layers as attention over training experience to help interpret test-time predictions.

paragraphs: Optimal transport turns distances between features into distances between samples. The feature-level distance, called the ground metric, therefore strongly shapes the resulting sample geometry. Choosing it is difficult without labels, and the paper addresses how to learn this metric directly from data in an unsupervised setting.

The proposed approach computes distances between samples and distances between features simultaneously. These two distance matrices arise as positive singular vectors of the function that maps ground metrics to optimal-transport distances. This provides a coupled mathematical construction for the two geometries. The authors give criteria ensuring that the singular vectors exist and are unique, so those properties depend on satisfying the stated criteria.

For high-dimensional settings, the paper develops scalable approximation methods based on stochastic approximation and entropic regularization. It then demonstrates Wasserstein Singular Vectors on a single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset. The contribution combines a principled unlabeled formulation with computational methods for approximating it, allowing the data to inform the feature distances on which optimal transport relies.
icml-2022-unsupervised-ground-metric-lea.tldr: Wasserstein Singular Vectors jointly learn sample and feature distances without labels, with conditional existence and uniqueness guarantees and scalable approximations.
